title: Dengue fever
text: Dengue presents with high fever, severe headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgia, and rash. Warning signs prompting hospital admission include abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, clinical fluid accumulation, mucosal bleeding, lethargy, liver enlargement over 2 cm, and a rising haematocrit with rapidly falling platelet count. Management in the absence of warning signs is outpatient with oral rehydration, paracetamol for fever, and avoidance of NSAIDs and aspirin because of bleeding risk. Platelet transfusion is not indicated for asymptomatic thrombocytopenia alone. Daily monitoring of haematocrit and platelet count is advised until 48 hours after fever resolves, spanning the critical defervescence period.

title: Malaria
text: Malaria in India is caused predominantly by Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium falciparum. Rapid diagnostic testing or microscopy should be performed in every febrile patient from an endemic area. Uncomplicated P. vivax is treated with chloroquine plus primaquine for radical cure after G6PD testing, since primaquine can cause haemolysis in G6PD-deficient patients. Uncomplicated P. falciparum is treated with an artemisinin-based combination per the national programme. Severe malaria (impaired consciousness, convulsions, respiratory distress, jaundice, or a parasite count above 4 percent) requires injectable artesunate and inpatient care.

title: Typhoid (enteric fever)
text: Enteric fever presents with stepladder fever, relative bradycardia, abdominal discomfort, and constipation or diarrhoea. Blood culture is the reference diagnostic test in the first week of illness; the Widal test alone is unreliable in endemic areas because of background seropositivity. First-line therapy is a third-generation cephalosporin or azithromycin given rising fluoroquinolone resistance in South Asia. Complications include intestinal perforation and gastrointestinal bleeding, which should be suspected with sudden worsening abdominal pain.

title: Pulmonary tuberculosis
text: Cough for more than two weeks, evening fever, night sweats, weight loss, and haemoptysis are classic presenting features. Sputum for CBNAAT (Cartridge-Based Nucleic Acid Amplification Test) is the preferred initial diagnostic under the National Tuberculosis Elimination Programme, followed by drug-susceptibility testing when rifampicin resistance is detected. Standard first-line therapy is a four-drug intensive phase (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) for two months followed by a continuation phase. Directly observed treatment and monthly follow-up improve completion rates; haemoptysis or drug-induced hepatitis during treatment both warrant prompt reassessment.

title: Chikungunya
text: Chikungunya causes abrupt high fever with severe, often symmetric, polyarthralgia that can persist for weeks to months after the acute febrile illness resolves. Distinguishing it from dengue matters because chikungunya rarely causes the plasma leakage or severe thrombocytopenia seen in dengue. Management is supportive: paracetamol for pain and fever, rest, and physical therapy for persistent arthralgia; NSAIDs are avoided until dengue has been excluded because of bleeding risk during the shared early febrile window.

title: Leptospirosis
text: Leptospirosis follows exposure to water or soil contaminated with animal urine and presents with abrupt fever, severe myalgia especially of the calves, conjunctival suffusion, and headache. Severe disease (Weil disease) produces jaundice, acute kidney injury, and pulmonary haemorrhage. Doxycycline is first-line for mild disease; severe disease requires intravenous penicillin or a third-generation cephalosporin plus supportive renal care, since delayed treatment materially worsens outcomes.

title: Scrub typhus
text: Scrub typhus, transmitted by chigger mite bites, presents with fever, headache, myalgia and, characteristically, an eschar at the bite site that is frequently missed on cursory examination. Untreated disease can progress to multi-organ dysfunction including myocarditis and acute respiratory distress. Doxycycline is first-line and produces rapid defervescence within 48 hours, which itself supports the diagnosis retrospectively.

title: Snakebite envenoming
text: Snakebite management begins with immobilising the affected limb, avoiding tourniquets and incision, and transporting the patient promptly to a facility stocking anti-snake venom. The 20-minute whole blood clotting test at the bedside screens for venom-induced coagulopathy from viperine bites. Neurotoxic envenoming from elapid bites (cobra, krait) produces ptosis, diplopia and progressive descending paralysis that can require ventilatory support. Polyvalent anti-snake venom is given for systemic envenoming, titrated to clinical and laboratory response rather than a fixed dose.

title: Organophosphate/pesticide poisoning
text: Organophosphate poisoning produces a cholinergic toxidrome: miosis, salivation, lacrimation, bronchorrhoea, bradycardia, and fasciculations, progressing to respiratory failure without treatment. Atropine is titrated aggressively to dry secretions, not to a fixed dose, and pralidoxime is given alongside atropine to reactivate acetylcholinesterase, most effective when started early. Airway protection and ventilatory support take priority when bronchorrhoea or respiratory muscle weakness is present; a cholinergic crisis can recur after apparent improvement (intermediate syndrome), so close monitoring continues for days.

title: Heat stroke
text: Heat stroke is a core temperature above 40C with altered mental status following heat exposure or exertion. Immediate aggressive cooling (evaporative cooling with tepid water and fanning, or ice-water immersion where feasible) is the single most important intervention and should not wait for transport. Antipyretics are not effective because the mechanism is not a hypothalamic set-point shift. Complications include acute kidney injury, rhabdomyolysis, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and hepatic injury, so laboratory monitoring continues even after the core temperature normalises.

title: Iron-deficiency anaemia in pregnancy
text: Iron-deficiency anaemia is highly prevalent among pregnant women in India and is screened for at every antenatal visit with a haemoglobin check. Oral iron and folic acid supplementation is first-line for mild to moderate anaemia; severe anaemia (haemoglobin below 7 g/dL) or intolerance to oral iron warrants parenteral iron. Blood transfusion is reserved for severe anaemia with cardiovascular compromise or near-term delivery. Untreated anaemia in pregnancy raises the risk of preterm birth, low birth weight, and postpartum haemorrhage.

title: COPD from biomass and air pollution exposure
text: Chronic exposure to biomass cooking smoke and ambient air pollution is a major driver of COPD in India, including in patients who have never smoked tobacco. Presentation is chronic cough, sputum production, and progressive exertional breathlessness. Spirometry showing a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio below 0.7 confirms fixed airflow obstruction. Management follows a stepwise approach: bronchodilators first, inhaled corticosteroids added for frequent exacerbations, pulmonary rehabilitation, and smoking or biomass-smoke-exposure cessation counselling, since continued exposure accelerates decline.

title: Type 2 diabetes mellitus
text: Type 2 diabetes carries a very high burden in India, often presenting at a younger age and lower body mass index than in Western populations. Diagnosis is confirmed by fasting plasma glucose at or above 126 mg/dL, HbA1c at or above 6.5 percent, or a 2-hour post-load glucose at or above 200 mg/dL, each ideally repeated for confirmation. Metformin is first-line pharmacotherapy alongside lifestyle modification; additional agents are added based on comorbidity, such as SGLT2 inhibitors or GLP-1 agonists where cardiovascular or renal disease coexists. Screening for retinopathy, nephropathy, and diabetic foot disease should occur at diagnosis and at regular intervals thereafter.

title: Hypertension
text: Hypertension is confirmed on two or more elevated readings on separate occasions, at or above 140/90 mmHg in the office setting. Lifestyle measures (salt restriction, weight management, physical activity) are advised at every stage. Pharmacotherapy typically starts with a single agent (ACE inhibitor, ARB, calcium channel blocker, or thiazide-like diuretic) and is escalated to combination therapy when target blood pressure is not reached. ACE inhibitors and ARBs are avoided in pregnancy. Home blood pressure monitoring improves control and detects white-coat and masked hypertension.

title: Acute gastroenteritis and cholera
text: Acute watery diarrhoea is managed primarily with oral rehydration solution; the priority is correcting and preventing dehydration rather than identifying a specific pathogen in most cases. Profuse rice-water stools with rapid dehydration raise suspicion for cholera, which in outbreak settings is managed with aggressive oral or intravenous rehydration and a single dose of doxycycline or azithromycin to shorten the carrier state. Antimotility agents are avoided in suspected invasive or bloody diarrhoea. Zinc supplementation is recommended alongside ORS in children.

title: Viral hepatitis A and E
text: Hepatitis A and E are faeco-orally transmitted and common causes of acute icteric hepatitis in India, often linked to contaminated water supply. Presentation is malaise, anorexia, nausea, right upper quadrant discomfort, and jaundice; most cases in otherwise healthy adults are self-limiting and managed supportively with rest, hydration, and avoidance of hepatotoxic drugs including unnecessary paracetamol dosing. Hepatitis E in pregnancy carries a materially higher risk of fulminant hepatic failure and warrants closer monitoring.

title: Rheumatic heart disease
text: Rheumatic heart disease follows one or more episodes of acute rheumatic fever after untreated group A streptococcal pharyngitis and remains disproportionately common in India. Acute rheumatic fever is diagnosed using the Jones criteria (carditis, polyarthritis, chorea, erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules as major criteria) alongside evidence of a preceding streptococcal infection. Secondary prophylaxis with regular benzathine penicillin injections prevents recurrent attacks and further valve damage, and is typically continued for years, sometimes lifelong when valve damage is established.

title: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) - analgesic/antipyretic
text: Paracetamol is the preferred antipyretic and analgesic in febrile illness where NSAIDs are contraindicated, including suspected dengue, because it does not impair platelet function. The maximum adult daily dose is 3 to 4 grams; exceeding this risks hepatotoxicity, particularly in patients with pre-existing liver disease or heavy alcohol use.

title: NSAIDs (ibuprofen, diclofenac) - analgesic/anti-inflammatory
text: NSAIDs are avoided in suspected dengue and other conditions with bleeding risk or thrombocytopenia because of platelet inhibition, and are used cautiously in chronic kidney disease, peptic ulcer disease, and in patients on anticoagulants because of additive bleeding and renal injury risk.

title: Doxycycline - tetracycline antibiotic
text: Doxycycline is first-line for leptospirosis, scrub typhus, and several other rickettsial and zoonotic infections common in India. It is avoided in pregnancy and in children under eight years except in specific severe-disease situations, because of effects on developing bone and tooth enamel.

title: Azithromycin - macrolide antibiotic
text: Azithromycin is used as an alternative first-line agent for enteric fever given rising fluoroquinolone resistance, and as a single-dose option in cholera. It prolongs the QT interval and should be used cautiously with other QT-prolonging drugs.

title: Ceftriaxone - third-generation cephalosporin
text: Ceftriaxone is first-line injectable therapy for enteric fever, severe leptospirosis, and many other serious bacterial infections. It should not be co-administered with calcium-containing intravenous solutions in neonates because of precipitation risk, and dose should be adjusted in significant renal impairment.

title: Metformin - biguanide antidiabetic
text: Metformin is first-line pharmacotherapy for type 2 diabetes. It is withheld in significant renal impairment (eGFR below about 30 mL/min/1.73m2) and temporarily around procedures using iodinated contrast, because of a rare but serious risk of lactic acidosis in that setting.

title: ACE inhibitors (enalapril, ramipril) - antihypertensive
text: ACE inhibitors are first-line for hypertension, particularly with coexisting diabetic nephropathy or heart failure. They are contraindicated in pregnancy because of fetal renal toxicity, and require monitoring of potassium and creatinine after initiation because of hyperkalaemia and acute kidney injury risk, especially when combined with NSAIDs or potassium-sparing diuretics.

title: Primaquine - antimalarial (radical cure)
text: Primaquine achieves radical cure of P. vivax malaria by clearing hepatic hypnozoites, but can cause severe haemolysis in G6PD-deficient patients. G6PD testing is recommended before primaquine when feasible; it is avoided in pregnancy and in infants under six months.

title: Oral and parenteral iron - haematinic
text: Oral iron is first-line for iron-deficiency anaemia including in pregnancy, with common gastrointestinal side effects (constipation, nausea) that reduce adherence. Parenteral iron is used for severe anaemia, intolerance to oral therapy, or when rapid correction is needed close to delivery.

title: Insulin - antidiabetic
text: Insulin is indicated in type 2 diabetes when oral agents fail to achieve glycaemic targets, in acute illness or hospitalisation, and is required in type 1 diabetes and most pregnancies complicated by diabetes because oral agents are generally avoided in pregnancy.

title: NSAIDs with anticoagulants
text: Combining NSAIDs with warfarin or direct oral anticoagulants substantially raises gastrointestinal and systemic bleeding risk through additive platelet and mucosal effects; an alternative analgesic such as paracetamol should be used where possible.

title: ACE inhibitors/ARBs with potassium-sparing diuretics
text: Co-administration of an ACE inhibitor or ARB with spironolactone or another potassium-sparing diuretic raises the risk of dangerous hyperkalaemia, particularly in chronic kidney disease; potassium and renal function should be monitored closely if the combination is clinically necessary.

title: Metformin around iodinated contrast
text: Metformin is temporarily withheld before and after procedures using iodinated intravenous contrast in patients with reduced renal function, because acute contrast-induced kidney injury combined with metformin accumulation can precipitate lactic acidosis.

title: Macrolides (azithromycin) with other QT-prolonging drugs
text: Azithromycin and other macrolides prolong the QT interval; combining them with antiarrhythmics, antipsychotics, or other QT-prolonging agents raises torsades de pointes risk, and caution is warranted in patients with baseline QT prolongation or electrolyte derangement.

title: Aspirin/NSAIDs in suspected dengue
text: Aspirin and NSAIDs are avoided in suspected or confirmed dengue because of the combination of thrombocytopenia and platelet dysfunction with plasma leakage, which materially raises bleeding risk during the critical phase of illness.

title: Penicillin allergy and cephalosporins
text: Patients with a history of penicillin allergy have a small but real risk of cross-reactivity with cephalosporins, higher for earlier-generation agents; a documented severe reaction (anaphylaxis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome) should prompt avoidance of the entire beta-lactam class pending allergy work-up, while a mild remote reaction may not preclude cautious use.

title: Sulfonamide allergy
text: A documented sulfonamide allergy should prompt avoidance of sulfonamide antibiotics such as co-trimoxazole; cross-reactivity with non-antibiotic sulfonamide-containing drugs (some diuretics, sulfonylureas) is debated and lower risk but still worth noting in the chart.
